summary: Specifies a simple file storage service run by UC Santa Barbara for other ARPANET users. After logging in, a user could allocate, update, replace, retrieve, space, delete and rename files with short primitive operations. It is a site-specific service description from 1971.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 122 describes a small remote storage service at UCSB in 1971. After logging in, users could reserve space, put files in, read them back, skip through them, rename them, or delete them using short coded commands.

subtitle: A 1971 site-specific service at UC Santa Barbara that offered simple remote file storage with a small set of binary commands.

tldr.problem: ARPANET users needed a place to store files, and UCSB wanted to make a limited amount of secondary storage available.
tldr.mechanism: The Simple-Minded File System listened on socket X'401' at site 3, used ICP to log in and establish two connections. It accepted binary commands (allocate, update, replace, retrieve, space, delete, rename, plus no-ops) with flags, and returned completion codes for each command.
tldr.outcome: SMFS was a site-specific service description (status Unknown), not a general FTP. UCSB noted it did not expect to be the Network's file storage node. It was later updated by RFC 217, 269, 399 and 431.

today: RFC 122 is a site-specific service description with status Unknown; it was updated by RFC 217, RFC 269, RFC 399 and RFC 431.

sections.title: The Simple-Minded File System
sections.content:
RFC 122 describes UCSB's Simple-Minded File System (SMFS), a site-specific service addressed at socket X'401', site 3. Files were stored on IBM 2316 disks and backed up to tape daily. UCSB explicitly stated it did not expect to become the file storage node of the Network, only to make a limited amount of secondary storage available.

The implementation notes mention that files could be up to 25 million bits in size and the system could serve up to ten users simultaneously (an assembly parameter).
sections.plainLanguage: It was a small shared storage closet run by one university for others on the ARPANET, not intended to hold everyone's files.

sections.title: Logging In
sections.content:
To use SMFS, a user opened an ICP connection to socket X'401' at site 3. SMFS accepted the call, sent back a 32-bit receive socket number n, then closed that connection. It then opened two connections to the user: one from its send socket n+1 to the user's receive socket m, and one from its receive socket n to the user's send socket m+1. Once both were established, the user was logged in.

SMFS kept connections open indefinitely and closed them only if it encountered a bad op code or to signal end-of-data. Users closed their connections when finished.
sections.plainLanguage: You knock on a known door, get told which two private doors to use for sending and receiving, and talk through those until you're done.

sections.title: Files and Operations
sections.content:
Files were sequential binary files from one bit up to 25 million bits. Filenames were 1 to 36 characters from A-Z, 0-9, blank (case-insensitive; EBCDIC or ASCII accepted). Each file could have an access password and a modification password checked separately for retrieval and changes.

SMFS supported: ALF (allocate filename/space/passwords), UDF (update/append data), RPF (replace contents), RTF (retrieve), SPF (space/skip a segment without sending data), DLF (delete), RNF (rename), FNO (file no-op to reset position), and NOP (discarded). Only one user could modify a file at a time; many could retrieve it concurrently. Formatted files could optionally preserve segment boundaries for retrieval.
sections.plainLanguage: You can reserve space, add to a file, replace it, read it back, skip ahead, delete it, or rename it. Passwords can restrict who reads or who changes the file.

sections.title: Command and Response Streams
sections.content:
Commands were binary messages starting with an 8-bit op code and a 16-bit flags field, followed only by the fields that command defined (filename, passwords, new filename, bit count, data). Filenames/passwords carried an 8-bit length first. SMFS maintained accumulators so fields could default to previous values if flags allowed (reducing redundant data). A null password was indicated by specific flag settings.

Every command except FNO and NOP produced a response containing the echoed op code and filename (unless suppressed), a completion code, and possibly bit count and data. Success returned a code equal to the op code; errors used codes such as 32 (file not found), 35 (incorrect password), 42 (end-of-data). An invalid op code was treated as severe: SMFS sent X'FF' followed by the bad op code, then closed both connections.
sections.plainLanguage: You send short coded messages, and the service replies to each with a code saying whether it worked and sometimes with data. If you send something it doesn't understand, the conversation ends.
